issues.title: Enterprise TLS interception breaks `Require-PQ-Auth` enforcement
issues.author: yaronf
issues.body:
## Summary

Enterprise TLS interception (and other non-built-in roots) will break
`Require-PQ-Auth` enforcement unless UAs can skip the pin for those
chains. David flagged this as deployment-blocking.

## Proposal

Add an exception along the lines of RFC 7469 §2.6 (Validating Pinned
Connections):

> It is acceptable to allow Pin Validation to be disabled for some Hosts
> according to local policy. For example, a UA may disable Pin Validation
> for Pinned Hosts whose validated certificate chain terminates at a
> user-defined trust anchor, rather than a trust anchor built-in to the UA
> (or underlying platform).

Normative home: Enforcement (and a short Security Considerations note).

## Scope

- In: MAY skip PQ-policy enforcement when the validated chain ends at a
  user-defined / non-built-in trust anchor (local policy).
- Out: changing what counts as a quantum-resistant Web PKI trust anchor;
  enterprise migration schedules (already out of scope in the appendix).

## References

- https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7469.html#section-2.6
- David’s review note on interception boxes / non-Web-PKI roots

issues.title: Sticky key-agreement under Require-PQ-Auth adds little benefit
issues.author: yaronf
issues.body:
## Summary

`Require-PQ-Auth` currently also requires quantum-resistant key
agreement. That coupling has little payoff for this temporary pin.

- The core value of the draft is stopping classical trust-anchor
  impersonation during the dual-trust-store period: a CRQC forges a
  classical certificate offline, and the holder presents it as the
  server. That attack does not depend on the negotiated key agreement.
  So even if KE is still classical (or misconfigured), the
  authentication pin still adds security against the threat this
  document targets. Breaking classical KE in a live session is a
  different, harder problem (a real-time CRQC); hybrid / PQ KE
  addresses it on its own track.
- Sticky KE enforcement does not usefully detect server
  misconfiguration. It only fails closed for clients that already have
  the pin; it does not give operators a clear config signal.

## Proposal

Drop key agreement from `Require-PQ-Auth` (auth-only pin). Remove KE
from the abstract, threat model, definitions, server commitment,
`{{pq-checks}}`, enforcement, and migration tables as needed. Hybrid /
PQ KE remains on its own deployment track.

Add a security consideration about KE: required for complete
quantum-resistance, but orthogonal to our solution.

## References

- David’s review note on simplifying away KE
- Draft threat model / `{{pq-checks}}` KE bullet

issues.title: Remove non-ASCII characters from the draft
issues.author: yaronf
issues.body:
## Summary

The rendered text has 33 lines with non-ASCII characters (idnits warning). Almost all are editorial; they should be ASCII for RFC-style source.

## Inventory (current txt)

- Em dash (`—`, U+2014): ~31 — body prose and stage titles
- Almost equal (`≈`, U+2248): 2 — Ops Considerations TODO (`public Web ≈ MTC`, `enterprise ≈ X.509`)
- Sharp s (`ß`, U+00DF): 1 — bibliography author name (`Klaußner`) pulled in at build from a referenced draft

The markdown source has the em dashes and the two `≈`; the `ß` comes from bibxml/reference expansion.

## Proposal

- Replace em dashes with ASCII punctuation (comma, colon, semicolon, hyphen, or parentheses) as fits each sentence.
- Replace `≈` with ASCII (e.g. `~` or `approx.`).
- For the bibliography `ß`: prefer an ASCII spelling if the reference tooling allows, or accept it as external metadata and document the exception.

No normative behavior change.

pulls.title: Complete Server Processing section
pulls.author: yaronf
pulls.body:
## Summary
- Replaces the Server Processing TODO with normative server commitment rules for `Require-PQ-Auth` (CRQC-resistant trust-anchor path + key agreement).
- Adds guidance for `max-age`, `include-subdomains`, and `preload`, plus HTTPS-only emission and `max-age=0` clearing caveats.

@davidben @tireddy2 — please review.

comments.author: tireddy2
comments.body:
The text on clearing the policy with max-age=0 is misleading. A browser that has noted the policy rejects any connection that doesn't meet it. So the browser can only receive max-age=0 over a connection that still meets the policy.

Example: a server sends max-age of one year. Three months later it loses its PQ certificate and can only serve a classical one. It now sends max-age=0, but every browser that noted the policy rejects the connection before any HTTP response arrives. None of them ever sees the max-age=0, so they cannot reach the server for the next nine months.

So:

max-age=0 only works if the server sends it while it can still meet the policy. The server should keep meeting the policy until the pins it already sent have expired.
If the server loses that ability first, there is no way to recover. Browsers stay locked out until the policy expires.

The promise should cover every server that answers for the hostname, not just the one that sent the header. That includes all CDN edges, failover or backup providers, and HTTP/3 endpoints advertised via Alt-Svc. If any of them cannot meet the policy, UAs that reach it will fail to connect.
The text says where to send the header, but not how often. Suggest saying the server should send it on every HTTPS response, as is common practice for HSTS.
The exception needs to be justified.
what do you mean by "exception", is it SHOULD vs. MUST?
Yes. If “SHOULD” is used, the document should provide justification for the exception and specify when it can be ignored.

The sections below are fine but I think there's more. Specifically hijacked TLS-terminating proxies as an attack vector - I think the highest risk is when they *add* a PQ-HSTS header and cause a server to be effectively bricked for a large client population.

Agreed, this is the main risk. Today the UA notes the header over any error-free TLS connection, including one with traditional authentication. So a hijacked proxy that has only a traditional certificate can add the header, and the host is bricked immediately.

Proposal: the UA notes Require-PQ-Auth only over a connection that satisfies the enforcement rules, that is, with CRQC-resistant authentication. This is similar to HPKP, which only noted pins that matched the connection’s validated chain (RFC 7469, Section 2.5). A proxy without a CRQC-resistant path can then no longer set the policy. 
The remaining risk is a proxy with a CRQC-resistant path setting a long max-age.

If you agree, I’ll update the UA noting rules and add a Denial of Service subsection covering both points.

I agree and this is a bug. In fact I thought we already had this rule. So yes, please add it and the DoS subsection.

There's a residual risk of a malicious proxy presenting a PQC cert that it obtained temporarily from an ACME server and then bricking the server after deleting the cert. But that's easy to detect and easy to mitigate.

And my AI adds for the DoS discussion:

1. Noting = full enforcement, not auth-only — You wrote “CRQC-resistant authentication.” Enforcement also needs non-mixed path + CRQC-resistant KE. Noting should require the same trio; otherwise a MitM with a PQ cert but classical-only KE can still set the pin and brick KE-incapable origin edges.

1. include-subdomains amplifies injection — One injected header with subdomain scope can pin the whole tree; call that out in DoS.

1. Preload is out of band — The noting fix does not help a poisoned PQ preload list; say so if DoS discusses preload.

1. Enterprise interception (availability, not injection) — After a legitimate pin, a non-PQ TLS middlebox breaks clients; different threat from hijacked-proxy injection, but operators care.
Fixed.

pulls.author: davidben
pulls.body:
The RFC editor is going to ask for PQ and HSTS to be expanded. Expanding the former is pretty reasonable. The latter would be unwieldy. Let's get ahead of that and pick a less fraught title.

pulls.title: Enterprise TLS interception carve-out for Require-PQ-Auth
pulls.author: yaronf
pulls.body:
## Summary
- Allow UAs to skip `Require-PQ-Auth` enforcement under local policy when the chain ends at a user-defined trust anchor (RFC 7469 §2.6 style), so classical enterprise interception roots do not fail closed for every Known PQ Host.
- Note the residual: where enforcement is skipped, the pin provides no protection; update Security Considerations accordingly.
- Closes #6.

cc @davidben (raised in review; not yet a repo collaborator)

Made with [Cursor](https://cursor.com)

comments.body:
Two comments.

1. Who disables and who checks. Such middleboxes are deployed and managed by the enterprise, and so are the UAs behind them. The enterprise can disable Require-PQ-Auth enforcement on its managed UAs through enterprise policy.
2. The protection does not have to be lost either. The middlebox is the TLS client to the origin. It can apply the checks in {{pq-checks}} on its connection to the origin, and note and enforce Require-PQ-Auth itself. The UA skips enforcement on the connection to the middlebox, while the middlebox enforces the policy on the connection to the origin. Suggest saying so, instead of “this mechanism provides no protection on that connection”.

TLS calls these devices middleboxes ({{Section 9.3 of RFC9846}}: “A middlebox which terminates a TLS connection MUST behave as a compliant TLS server (to the original client)”). The draft currently says “TLS-terminating proxy”, “interception device” and “TLS interceptor”. Suggest using “middlebox that terminates TLS” throughout.

1. As discussed, these are not always "boxes" and they may not be managed by the enterprise.
2. Agree, but the text will be somewhat vague because you cannot force someone to implement an RFC.
Agree.

This is very long. I think two sentences are enough:

> The UA MAY skip enforcement according to local policy. For example, similar to {{Section 2.6 of ?RFC7469}}, the UA MAY skip enforcement if the validated certificate chain terminates as a user-defined trust anchor, rather than a trust anchor built-in to the UA (or underlying platform).

I suggest we simply delete this paragraph. The original one missed the point a bit. The problem isn't that the TLS interceptor can cause a denial of service. It doesn't need to intercept TLS for that and can just close the connection. That's not interesting.

The notable thing is that TLS interceptor can *persistently* cause a DoS, even after it stops being on path on the network, or stops being able to intercept TLS.

pulls.title: Drop key agreement from Require-PQ-Auth
pulls.author: yaronf
pulls.body:
## Summary
- Make `Require-PQ-Auth` auth-only: remove quantum-resistant key agreement from the abstract, threat model, definitions, server commitment, connection checks, and migration tables.
- Add Security Considerations explaining that complete quantum resistance still needs QR KE, but it is orthogonal; the pin still helps if KE is misconfigured.
- Closes #8.

cc @davidben (raised in review; not yet a repo collaborator)

Made with [Cursor](https://cursor.com)

comments.body: Suggest adding to the Key Agreement subsection: “With quantum-resistant authentication, a CRQC attacker cannot downgrade the negotiated key agreement {{?RFC9958}}.”
The text is fine, but the reference is kind of open-ended. Do you have a particular section in mind?
Optional: In the interest of making the document shorter, I'd actually suggest just removing this paragraph altogether. I'm not sure it adds anything to the introduction.
Also in the interest of trimming unnecessary text, I'd suggest just deleting this whole paragraph too.

Existing issue, but "comparatively well-understood" is a but subjective. Why not simply:

> This mechanism addresses classical trust-anchor impersonation during the dual-trust-store-period.

(LLMs talk too much.)

I'm not sure what "otherwise obtains acceptance under a classical trust anchor" means, particular relative to what a CRQC can do.

I think simply "An attacker forges a classical certificate a CQRC, and presents [...]" is fine.
Let's just omit the last sentence.
(TBH I think we can just delete this whole section. It's just restating a fact about TLS that's not directly relevant to what this draft is doing.)

This last sentence is misleading. While it blocks a classical certificate chain, it doesn't mean much. If you use classical key agreement with post-quantum authentication, the attacker can just break the key agreement, reconstruct the key schedule, and break your connection that way.

Instead, I suggest replacing this section with one that discusses this:

> Quantum resistance for a TLS session also requires a quantum-resistent key agreement mechanism. While `Request-PQ-Auth` does not directly constrain the key agreement, the TLS handshake provides downgrade protection when the authentication itself is secure. See {{Appendix F.1 of !RFC9846}}. Provided the Known PQ Host's TLS server is correctly configured to prefer quantum-resistant key agreement methods, a CRQC cannot downgrade the TLS session to a classical key agreement mechanism.
This seems redundant iwth the other section. Suggest just removing it.
Suggest just not saying anything about key agreement, in the interest of reducing the word count.

Here I disagree. A real-time break of a live key exchange is a lot more challenging that an off-line break of a certificate. (Yes this is all speculative but still IMHO very likely.) So there's value in PQ-HSTS even if the key exchange is for some reason non-QR.

pulls.title: Trim the discussion of preload
pulls.author: davidben
pulls.body: Fundamentally, there is nothing useful we can say about preload here other than "the UA can have some local policy if it wants", so leave it at that. Preload is not a panacea, particular for this as compared to HSTS.

pulls.title: Remove the restating of ChromiumPQAuthRoadmap
pulls.author: davidben
pulls.body:
I was going to give it a rewrite but this document is too long and too AI-generated right now. I don't think restating it, but differently and less accurately, in this document provides any value over just citing the original document.

Just trim this for now, given the submission deadline. We can add a longer discussion if we need to later. But really the main thing that needs to be said about the broader context is that this is a temporary, short-term, and very limited measure. That's covered in the new Limitations section, which will hopefully be easier to find once excess text is trimmed away.

In doing so, also trim some of the excess sections in the introduction. Those kept restating what was already in the introduction. I've retained the text pointing to I-D.sheffer-tls-pqc-continuity, but instead moved it to Acknowledgements.

pulls.title: Edit the abstract and introduction a bit
pulls.author: davidben
pulls.body:
authors.ietf.org talks about making the abstract self-contained, so avoid defining it relative to HSTS. The intro similarly doesn't need a long comparison to HSTS. The concept is simple enough that we can introduce it on its own.

Briefly call out the limitations in the introduction, so the reader has broader context.

pulls.title: Rework the core of the document a bit
pulls.author: davidben
pulls.body:
Some minor shortening of text, but the main thing is getting to a crisper definition of what's in scope. That crisper definition is, unfortunately, "this is up to the application". This is unavoidable because the application may have all manner of PKI policies. This avoids the difficulty the older text had with MTCs.

Also fix some other issues like... the server actually still needs to serve a classical certificate to old clients.
